extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, compositors, and typesetters working on book and journal production
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and guidance for punctuation, hyphenation, word divisions, footnote and reference formatting, indexing, and tabular composition for formal publishing. Intended to be applied by editors, proofreaders, and compositors preparing manuscripts for print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the dash with punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should not ordinarily be used in connection with any other point, except a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Correct: "DEAR SIR: I have the honor . . . ."; not: "DEAR SIR:— I have . . . ." Correct: "This — I say it with regret — was not done"; not: "This, — I say it with regret, — was . . . ."

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses for in-text enumeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Place between parentheses figures or letters used to mark divisions in enumerations run into the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "The reasons for his resignation were three: (i) advanced age, (2) failing health, (3) a desire to travel." If divisions are paragraphed, use a single parenthesis ordinarily with a lower-case (italic) letter; use a period with figures and capital (roman) letters. A standard indentation/notation scheme (A., I., 1., a), (1), (a), etc.) is recommended for syllabi and similar matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses for parenthetical clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses should not ordinarily be used for parenthetical clauses unless confusion would arise from less distinctive marks or the clause is wholly irrelevant to the main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Acceptable: "He meant — I take this to be the (somewhat obscure) sense of his speech — that . . . ."; "The period thus inaugurated (of which I shall speak at greater length in the next chapter) was characterized by ...." Use parentheses sparingly for parenthetical remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses of brackets
rubrics_metrics.description: Brackets are used (1) to inclose an explanation or note, (2) to indicate an interpolation in a quotation, (3) to rectify a mistake, (4) to supply an omission, and (5) for parentheses within parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Editorial note: [This was written before the publication of Spencer's book. — EDITOR.]; Interpolation: "These [the free-silver Democrats] asserted ..."; Rectify: "As the Italian [Englishman] Dante Gabriel Rossetti has said ..."; supply omission in bibliographic citation examples. Use brackets for nested parenthetical material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracketed continuation/series notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases such as "To be continued," and "Continued from ..." at the ends or beginnings of articles or chapters should be placed between brackets, centered, set in italics, and in type reduced in size according to rules governing reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: [Continued from p. 320]  [To be concluded]

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses to indicate omissions and lacunae
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses are used to indicate omission from a quotation of words not essential to the idea being conveyed, and to indicate illegible words, mutilations, and other lacunae in quoted material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an ellipsis at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence, ordinarily use four periods separated by a space (en quad), except in very narrow measures (French: three). If the preceding line ends in a point, do not include it in the four. When whole paragraphs or lines (in poetry) are omitted, insert a full line of periods separated by em- or 2-em quads according to line length; periods should not extend beyond the length of the longest type-line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses in citations
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis should be treated as part of the citation and therefore should be enclosed in the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the rule for quotation punctuation: include the ellipsis inside the closing quotation marks when it belongs to the quoted material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen: general functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is placed at the end of a line terminating with a syllable carried to the next line and between many compound words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See detailed hyphenation rules for compounds, adjectival phrases, and line-break hyphenation practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compound adjectives before a noun
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate two or more words combined into one adjective preceding a noun, or when the noun is understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: so-called Croesus, well-known author, first-class investment, better-trained teachers, nineteenth-century progress, up-to-date machinery, four-year-old boy. Do not hyphenate when the adjective follows the noun or when adverbs ending in -ly modify the adjective (e.g., highly developed species).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation with multiword components: use en dash
rubrics_metrics.description: Where one of the components contains more than one word, an en dash should be used in place of a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York–Chicago freight traffic; Norwegian–German–Jewish immigrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not hyphenate adverb (-ly) + adjective
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not connect adjectives or participles with adverbs ending in '-ly' by hyphens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: highly developed species; a man well known in the neighborhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate nouns formed by two nouns in objective relation
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, hyphenate nouns formed by the combination of two nouns standing in objective relation to each other (one component derived from a transitive verb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mind-reader, story-teller, office-holder, hero-worship, wood-turning. Exceptions include common brief compounds such as lawgiver, taxpayer, proofreader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate present participle + noun or absolute prepositional phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: A present participle united with a noun to form a new noun with a distinct meaning, or with a preposition used absolutely to form a noun, should have a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: boarding-house, dining-hall, sleeping-room, walking-stick, working-man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds with book/house/mill/room/shop/work: syllable-based rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds with 'book', 'house', 'mill', 'room', 'shop', and 'work' should generally be printed as one word when the prefixed noun has one syllable, hyphenated when it has two, and printed as two separate words when it has three or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: handbook, schoolbook; pocket-book, story-book; reference book. Exceptions for appearance or rare combinations (e.g., source-book).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds denoting occupations: hyphenate
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'maker', 'dealer', and other words denoting occupation should ordinarily be hyphenated, as also nouns denoting different occupations of the same individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: harness-maker, book-dealer, job-printer; a soldier-statesman, the poet-artist Rossetti. Short everyday exceptions: bookmaker, dressmaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'store' hyphenation by syllable count
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'store' should be hyphenated when the prefix contains only one syllable; otherwise not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: drug-store, feed-store (but: bookstore); grocery store, dry-goods store.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'fellow' always hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'fellow' are always hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fellow-man, fellow-beings, play-fellow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family-relation compounds hyphenation as first element
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'father', 'mother', 'brother', 'sister', 'daughter', 'parent', and 'foster' should be hyphenated when forming the first element of the compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: father-love (but: fatherland), mother-tongue, foster-son. Observe exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'great-' for fourth-degree descent
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'great' indicating the fourth degree in a direct line of descent call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: great-grandfather, great-grandson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compounds with 'life' and 'world'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'life' and 'world' require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: life-history, life-principle (but: lifetime), world-power, world-problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'skin' by syllable count
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'skin' with words of one syllable are printed as one word; with words of more than one syllable, printed as two separate words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: calfskin, sheepskin; alligator skin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'master' hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'master' should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: master-builder, master-stroke (exception: masterpiece).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds with 'god' when second element: hyphenate
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'god' forms the second element of a compound, the compound should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sun-god, rain-god (but: godsend, godson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'half-' and 'quarter-' combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Half', 'quarter', etc., combined with a noun should be followed by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: half-truth, half-tone, half-year, quarter-mile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefixes semi-/demi-/bi-/tri- ordinarily no hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Semi-', 'demi-', 'bi-', 'tri-', etc., do not ordinarily demand a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: semiannual, demigod, biweekly, trimonthly. Exceptions for long or unusual formations (e.g., semi-centennial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds with 'self-' hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds with 'self' as the first element are hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: self-evident, self-respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations with 'fold' print as one word if one-syllable number, otherwise two words
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations with 'fold' are one word if the number contains one syllable; if the number contains more, print as two words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: twofold, tenfold; fifteen fold, a hundred fold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives formed with 'like' hyphenation by noun syllable count
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives formed by suffixing 'like' to a noun are usually one word if the noun contains one syllable (except when ending in /); if the noun contains more syllables or is a proper noun, they should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: childlike, homelike; eel-like, bell-like; woman-like, American-like (but: Christlike).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate parts of titles such as 'vice-', 'ex-', 'elect', etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Particles forming parts of titles should be connected to the chief noun by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vice-Consul Taylor, ex-President Cleveland, the governor-elect, the postmaster-general, a lieutenant-colonel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compounds beginning with 'by-'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds beginning with 'by-' should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: by-product, by-laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation for co-, pre-, re- before same vowel or w/y
rubrics_metrics.description: The prefixes 'co-', 'pre-', and 're-' take a hyphen when followed by the same vowel as that in which they terminate, or by w or y; otherwise as a rule they do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: co-operation, pre-empted, re-enter, co-worker, re-yield; but: cooperate, coequal, prearranged, reinstal. Exceptions: proper names, long/unusual formations, or where omission changes meaning (e.g., re-cover vs. recover).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit hyphen in today/tomorrow/tonight/viewpoint/standpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the hyphen in common compound adverbial/time words such as 'today', 'tomorrow', 'tonight', and in viewpoint/standpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to related notes (see 119).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative particles un-, in-, a- usually no hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: The negative particles 'un-', 'in-', and 'a-' do not usually require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unmanly, undemocratic, inanimate, asymmetrical. Exceptions are rare/artificial combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non- ordinarily hyphenated (but common words exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: The particle 'non-' ordinarily calls for a hyphen, except in the commonest words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: non-aesthetic, non-subservient, non-unionist; but: nonage, nondescript, nonessential, nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi- requires hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Quasi-' prefixed to a noun or an adjective requires a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quasi-corporation, quasi-historical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over- and under- prefixes generally not hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Over' and 'under' prefixed to a word should not be followed by a hyphen, except in unusual cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: overbold, overemphasize, overweight, underfed, undersecretary; exceptions: over-soul, under-man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin prepositional prefixes generally no hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: The Latin prepositions 'ante', 'anti', 'inter', 'intra', 'post', 'sub', and 'super' prefixed to a word do not ordinarily require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: antedate, antechamber, antidote, international, intramural (but: intra-atomic). Exceptions include forms like ante-bellum, anti-Semitic, inter-university.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra/infra/pan/supra/ultra generally hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Extra', 'infra', 'pan', 'supra', and 'ultra' as a rule call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: extra-hazardous, infra-mundane, pan-Hellenic, ultra-conservative (but: Ultramontane).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fractions spelled out: hyphenate numerator and denominator
rubrics_metrics.description: In fractional numbers spelled out, connect by a hyphen the numerator and the denominator, unless either already contains a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: two-thirds, five-sevenths, thirty-hundredths; but thirty-one hundredths (no hyphen connecting groups when larger constructs). Do not hyphenate in constructions like 'one half of his fortune ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen to indicate omitted common element in series
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more compound words occurring together have a common component omitted from all but the last, indicate the omission by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in English- and German-speaking countries; one-, five-, and ten-cent pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen to indicate prefixes/suffixes as particles
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is used to indicate a prefix or suffix as a particle or syllable not complete in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The prefix a-'; 'The German diminutive suffixes -chen and -lein.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen employed to indicate syllables
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a hyphen to indicate syllabification of a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: di-a-gram, pho-tog-ra-phy.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of everyday words that should be hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain common everyday compounds that do not fit other classifications are to be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: after-years, bas-relief, birth-rate, blood-relations, coat-of-arms, common-sense, cross-examine, cross-reference, death-rate, food-stuff, fountain-head, guinea-pig, horse-power, loan-word, man-of-war, object-lesson, page-proof, pay-roll, post-office, sea-level, sense-perception, son-in-law, subject-matter, title-page, wave-length, well-being, will-power, well-nigh, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary divisions: general principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid all unnecessary divisions of words; wherever consistent with good spacing, carry the whole word over into the next line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good spacing is paramount; do not divide words unnecessarily for justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide very short syllables or words
rubrics_metrics.description: In wide measures (20 ems or more), do not divide on a syllable of two letters if possible; never carry over a syllable of two letters; words of four letters should never be divided; words of five or six letters rarely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions only when spacing demands it; prioritize readability over rigid division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit consecutive hyphenated line endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Never let more than two consecutive lines terminate in a hyphen if avoidable; avoid dividing the next-to-last line of a paragraph; the last line (breakline) in measures of 15 ems and up should contain at least four letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also avoid a divided word at the bottom of a right-hand (recto) page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide proper nouns or initials
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide proper nouns, especially names of persons, unless absolutely necessary. Do not separate initials of a name or combinations like A.D., P.M., etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep marks and identifiers with the material they pertain to; e.g., do not leave a divisional mark like (a) at the end of a line separated from the section it introduces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide according to pronunciation (American system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide words according to pronunciation (the American system), not derivation (the English system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: democ-racy not demo-cracy; knowledge not knowl-edge. However, where compatible with pronunciation and good spacing, it's acceptable to divide compounds on etymological lines (e.g., dis-pleasure rather than displeas-ure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division when two consonants meet between vowels
rubrics_metrics.description: When two consonants meet between vowels and the syllable ends on one consonant, dividing between the consonants is proper, pronunciation determining the division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: advan-tage, exces-sive, finan-cier, moun-tain, profes-sor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid terminal division on soft c, g, or j
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not terminate a line in a soft c, g, or j; avoid such division entirely if possible; if necessary, divide differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred divisions: pro-cess (not proc-ess), ne-cessary (not nec-essary), spacing (not spac-ing). Note this rule may differ from certain dictionaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide on a vowel where practicable; exceptions for -able/-ible
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel wherever practicable. If a vowel alone forms a syllable in the middle of a word, run it into the first line. Exceptions: words in -able and -ible should carry the vowel over into the next line (read-able, convert-ible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: separate (sepa-rate, not sep-arate); particular (particu-lar, not partic-ular).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid additional hyphens in hyphenated words when dividing
rubrics_metrics.description: In hyphenated nouns and adjectives, avoid introducing additional hyphens when dividing the word across lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: object-lesson (not object-les-son); fellow-being (not fel-low-being).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat diphthongs as single letters
rubrics_metrics.description: A coalition of two vowel-sounds into one (a diphthong) should be treated as one letter; do not divide between the vowels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: people should not be divided; Caesar (Cae-sar) handled as appropriate; building should not be bu-ilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division rules for derivatives from words ending in 't'
rubrics_metrics.description: In derivatives from words ending in t, the t, in divisions, should be carried into the next line with the suffix if the accent has been shifted; if the derivative has retained the accent of the parent-word, the t should remain in the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: objec-tive (from ob'ject), defect-ive (from defect'); but: respec-tively, distinc-tive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural -s does not create license to divide
rubrics_metrics.description: The addition of a plural s, adding a new syllable to words ending in an s-sound, does not justify dividing the word that would otherwise be unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hor-ses and circumstan-ces are impossible divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide adjectives in -ical on the 'i'
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives in -ical should be divided on the i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: physi-cal (not phys-ical nor physic-al).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide the word 'nothing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this as an absolute prohibition (see 230).

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensed foreign-language division rules: French
rubrics_metrics.description: For French, divide on a vowel as far as possible, avoiding consonantal ending of syllables; two consonants where second is l or r are carried over to following syllable; count as many syllables as vowels, except mute e after a vowel does not form a syllable; i,y,o,ou,u preceding other vowels often act as consonants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in-di-vi-si-bi-li-te; tableau (not tab-leau); balancer (not bal-ancer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensed foreign-language division rules: German
rubrics_metrics.description: For German, divide on a vowel as far as possible; if several consonants stand between vowels, usually only the last is carried over; combinations like sz, ch, sch, ph, st, th are never separated; if ck must be divided, separate into k-k; in foreign words certain consonant clusters with l or r are carried over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hütten (Hü-ten), Fabrik (Fa-brik), Ritter (Rit-ter); Deckel— Dek-kel for ck division; compounds separated into components first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensed foreign-language division rules: Italian
rubrics_metrics.description: For Italian, divide on a vowel as far as possible; certain consonant clusters (s before consonant, r following consonant, ch, gh, gli, gn, qu, sc, etc.) are never separated; i and u go with following vowel; some vowel combinations not separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ta-vo-li-no, nar-ra-re; castighi, uscire, migliori.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensed foreign-language division rules: Spanish
rubrics_metrics.description: For Spanish, divide on a vowel as far as possible; ch, ll, rr, ñ treated as single consonants; cc and nn are divided; liquid consonants l and r when preceded by another consonant should not be separated from it except in compounds; s is always disjoined from a following consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ca-ra-co-les, mu-cha-cho, pron-to, as-pi-rar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensed foreign-language division rules: Greek
rubrics_metrics.description: Single consonants and consonant combinations that can begin a word and certain mutes followed by p or b are placed at beginning of syllable; other consonant combinations are divided; compound words are divided into original parts first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given in Greek script (syllabification rules and compound division).

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensed foreign-language division rules: Latin
rubrics_metrics.description: Latin words have as many syllables as vowels or diphthongs; when a single consonant occurs between vowels, divide before the consonant; when two or more consonants occur, divide before the last consonant except in mute+liquid and qu/gu combinations; compound words are separated into components first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cae-sar, me-ri-di-es; omnis (om-nis), scriptus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote indices: use superior figures; other symbols only in special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: For reference indices, as a rule use superior (superscript) figures. Only in special cases should asterisks, daggers, etc., be used (e.g., in tabular or algebraic matter where figures would cause confusion). Place index figures in the text after punctuation marks, without space (except in German where they are placed inside).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When figures are not used, use sequence: * (asterisk), † (dagger), ‡ (double dagger), § (section mark), || (parallels), ¶ (paragraph mark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'ibid.', 'loc. cit.', 'op. cit.' in footnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Where references to the same work follow each other closely and uninterruptedly, use 'Ibid.' instead of repeating the title; 'Ibid.' takes the place of as much of the previous reference as is repeated. 'Ibid.' should not ordinarily be used for the first footnote on a verso page; better repeat the title if short or use 'loc. cit.' or 'op. cit.' as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show 'Ibid.' replacing a repeated citation; be cautious with page breaks and page sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes to tables: size and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes to tables, whether ruled or open, should be in 6-pt and should invariably be placed at the foot of the table and not at the foot of the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For indices in table footnotes use asterisks etc., not superior figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not repeat an author's name in footnote if given in text
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author's name is given in the text in connection with a reference to or a quotation from his work, it should not be repeated in the footnote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If text reads 'This theory is questioned by Herbert, as follows: "I cannot admit ..."', footnote should contain only the bibliographic details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of footnote index figure for quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to place the index figure in the text at the end of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the illustration in the manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit abbreviations Vol., chap., p. ordinarily in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily omit 'Vol.', 'chap.', and 'p.' in references to particular passages; use Roman numerals (capitals) for Volume, Book, Part, Division except for ancient/classical authors where lower-case roman numerals are used; use Arabic numerals for number (Heft) and text pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use 'Vol.', 'p.' etc., when confusion would arise or in exceptional cases; for classical references use periods instead of commas in divisions of works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date placement in periodical references
rubrics_metrics.description: The date of publication in a reference to a periodical should immediately follow the volume number and be put in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the provided illustrations for formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote numbering convention for Linotype set work
rubrics_metrics.description: In work set on the linotype machine, footnotes should be numbered consecutively through an article in a journal or through a chapter in a book to save resetting in case of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions exist (e.g., Botanical Gazette, Astrophysical Journal) which have adopted different styles and numbering schemes; consult house rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: treatment of Mac/Me/M'/St./Ste. prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Names beginning with Mac, Me, or M', St., Ste., whether the following letter is capitalized or not, should be listed as if the prefix were spelled Mac, Saint, Sainte to avoid scattering entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Machiavelli; St. Louis; MacIntyre, M'Intyre treatments shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: compound/hyphenated names listed under first part with cross-references
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound names should be listed under the first part of the name. List the other parts in their alphabetical positions with cross-references to the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Campbell-Bannerman, Sir Henry; Lloyd-George, David; provide cross-reference 'George, Lloyd-. See Lloyd-George.' For hyphenated names gratuitously adopted (e.g., married women adding maiden name), the name preceding the hyphen may be disregarded and listing under true name with cross-reference is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: prefixes treated under following part except specified exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Names with prefixes should be listed under the part following the prefix, except: (i) in English in certain cases; (ii) in French when prefix contains the article; (iii) in Italian/Spanish when prefix consists simply of the article; (iv) Dutch 'Van','Ten' etc. are always capitalized; (v) when prefix and name are written as one word. Naturalized names with prefixes follow the rules for the adopted language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and language-specific exceptions provided: Hoffman, von; Lima, de; Ponte e Horto, da; etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: umlauted characters and their sorting
rubrics_metrics.description: Names spelled with umlaut a, o, u should be listed as if the umlaut were spelled out ae, oe, ue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Müller should be treated as Mueller for alphabetical ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: names with connectors (and/&/y/et/und/e) list under first part
rubrics_metrics.description: Names having two parts or firm names connected by 'and', '&', 'y' (Spanish), 'et' (French), 'und' (German), or 'e' (Italian) should be listed according to the first letter of the name preceding the connective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Smith & Evans (under 'S'); Gomez y Pineda (under 'G'); Loubet et Meunier (under 'L').

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular type sizes and leading guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Open (unruled) and ruled tables have recommended type sizes and leading depending on the body matter type size: in 9-pt and 10-pt matter open tables set in 6-pt leaded, ruled in 8-pt solid; in 8-pt matter both open and ruled set in 8-pt solid; in 6-pt matter set in 6-pt solid. There's a practice of using different type in tables for totals, averages, percentages, and generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Italic and black-face figures may be used to set off various classes of results in table columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table captions and box-heads sizing and case
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions for columns of open tables and box-heads for ruled tables should ordinarily be set in 6-pt. In ruled tables with multi-story box-heads, primary heads set in caps and small caps (except where second story is figures only); secondary heads in caps and lower case. If small caps are used in box-heads, stub head should also be in caps and small caps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consistent visual hierarchy in table heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing between rules and table matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruled tables there should be at least two leads' space between the horizontal rules and the matter inclosed, and, if practicable, at least the equivalent of an en quad of the body type between perpendicular rules and inclosed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides clear breathing room inside ruled cells.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders and period alignment in tables
rubrics_metrics.description: In open tables either periods, one em apart and aligned, or leaders may be used between columns. In ruled tables, leaders should usually be employed in the stub if there is room. Use leaders across full column width to indicate blanks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'leader' is a piece of type with dots or short lines used to guide the eye across space to the right word or number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of numerals and reading-matter in table columns
rubrics_metrics.description: Center figures in figure columns; if exact centering is impossible and digit groups vary, leave more space on the left than on the right. When there is reading-matter in ruled-table columns, center it if possible; if lines run over, use hanging indentation and align all on the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for visual consistency and readability of numeric and textual table content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of double rules and open vs ruled table decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Double rules should be used at the top of all tables; vertical double rules used usually only when a table is doubled up on itself. Tables of two columns only should be set as open; three or more columns as ruled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these formatting conventions for table clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table numbering and headline formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Table I' etc. in table headlines should ordinarily be set in caps of the type in which the body of the table is set; the following descriptive line in caps and small caps. A single descriptive headline without a number should be set in caps of the table type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides consistent look for table headings and descriptive lines.
